items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Josh said he feels the fatigue?’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The Sixers beat the Knicks on Friday…

…meaning they are 2-0 in the head-to-head matchup. That’s it, that’s all it means. No parade down Broad Street.

Here’s what we heard coming out of Cheesesteak Arena.

On losing to the 76ers in the NBA Cup:

“I don’t look it as a statement game. It’s the next game in front of us. Obviously, it’s a [NBA] Cup game and you always want to push yourself to have an opportunity to try and win something. This means taking a step toward that goal.

“But I just want to get a little better every time we play. These guys really hurt us in transition last game. Our transition defense right now stinks. But it’s gotten a little better. Tonight, it will be tested. Obviously Jaylen is not playing and he’s one of the best in transition. You look at little things and you hope to get better at the little things while getting a win.”

On the Knicks allowing Philadelphia to attack the paint too easily:

“They were getting in our paint left and right, right and left, and it was really, really easy doing it.”

On the Knicks forcing difficult plays instead of executing simple offense:

“It’s been going on all year. Like, we’re trying to hit a home run every time we get the ball. And we have to hit singles. We can’t hit a home run. We gotta hit singles offensively and then if our play breaks down, we have to move. There’s too many times where we have too many guys trying to iso and the other four guys sitting there and staring at the ball a whole possession.”

On the Knicks improving their turnover management in the second half:

“We did a better job with our turnovers (in the second half). But more importantly, we reacted better when we turned the ball over and we had five turnovers for six points (against).”

On the Knicks failing to maintain their focus throughout an entire game:

“Against a good team on the road, if you let go of those things in a half, you’re in trouble. And so somehow some way we have to be cognizant of doing this stuff for 48 minutes, which we’re not doing right now.

“Tonight it was the first half and it was almost like [we thought] we’re just gonna show up and go hoop and not do the little things that we need to do to go get a win.”

On the importance of executing the fundamentals consistently:

“It’s a little thing here, a little thing there, a little thing there. … We’re competitive when we need to be and that’s why all of our games that we’re in we have a chance down the stretch, but trying to make sure we continue to do the little things throughout the course of the game is gonna be huge for us because we’re not doing it right now.”

On LeBron James making decisive plays against the Knicks:

“[LeBron’s] a great player, and when you have a great player out there, with his ability, he’s gonna make plays, and he made big plays down the stretch. It’s the NBA, and it’s not surprising when a guy like Maxey or LeBron or Jalen makes a big play. You just hope that it doesn’t come down to that all the time.”

On Ernie Johnson’s retirement announcement and his impact on NBA coverage:

“I’d like to give a quick shoutout to Ernie Johnson. I don’t know him well. Obviously I know him from the TV. I try not to watch a lot of basketball shows because it gets me too high or gets me too low. But their show is one that I always get good laughs at.

“Just from afar, Ernie seems like he’s a big time human being. And the little bit I know about his story, it’s fascinating. He will be sorely missed, not only from the fans out there and other media members, but I know from a coaching standpoint too in keeping everything light and enjoyable and all that other stuff.

“So I hope you have a heck of a year, Ernie. We’re gonna all miss you, but thanks for doing what you do to make people smile everyday.”

On the Knicks’ careless turnovers and hesitant decision-making:

“Just a little careless. And sometimes it can be us being hesitant as well, wanting to make the right play, but they’re also not trying to turn over, and then it’s just a little late to our decision-making. It could be a lot of things, but obviously, we got to clean it up.”

On Josh Hart’s fatigue excuse six games into the season:

“Josh said he feels the fatigue? Well, Josh is old as s–t, so.”

On the Knicks needing to learn from their losses and stop relying on comebacks:

“I’ve said in the past that it’s always important to learn from wins. Obviously, you learn from losses, as well. There have been plenty of times that we’ve learned from being down. In those same games, we’ve made adjustments to where we weren’t down anymore and came back and won the game. Obviously, we have to understand what we need to do. It’s starting the game that way. I think that has to be our biggest point of emphasis going forward.

“I thought we played decent in the second half, took care of the ball better, played better defense, but we have to put a full 48 minutes together.”

On the Knicks lacking energy against Philadelphia:

“Today we played like a team that was on the end of a road trip. We gotta find that gear. We gotta find that energy.

“We picked up the pace in the second half, but what makes this team special is doing it for 48 minutes. We didn’t do that tonight. We put ourselves in a bad spot, and give credit to the team over there. They hit the shots when they needed to. We just got to execute at a higher level.”

On escaping the Knicks’ offensive struggles too late against the 76ers:

“I thought we did a great job in that fourth quarter of finding that gear, like you said, just kind of getting out of the quicksand. To do that puts us in a position where you gotta make some magic happen, and we just didn’t have enough magic tonight.”

On the challenge of facing LeBron James and the 76ers:

“They’re a great team. Obviously, you have arguably the greatest player of all time. We’ve got to bring our best. We’ve got to execute at a high level. And we’ve got to continue to use these games as a learning experience.”

On the Knicks’ stagnant offense and lack of movement:

“It’s a new year. I think we’re trying to work our way into the season. But I think the flow’s tougher. Sometimes the ball is stagnant, I think that’s a little bit from fatigue and not a mental thing. You know what the other team is doing, and physically you’re trying to get your body to get to that point. So I think that that’s part of it. We got to be more deliberate with cuts and movements. And taking care of the ball.”

On the Knicks feeling fatigued after playing three games in four nights:

“We all feel the fatigue. So we got to fight through it. Six games in. So we got to find a way to make sure we get our bodies ready to play every day. I think mentally we’re there. We just gotta find it physically.”

On the Knicks needing to execute more consistently:

“We gotta find a way to execute better. And do that continuously.”

On why the Knicks keep falling behind by double digits before attempting comebacks:

“I wish I could tell you that one. If I could tell you that one, and the reason why, then maybe it would stop happening. I think we all have a great will to win. I think sometimes it takes us a little longer to find a game, whether that’s the flow, fatigue, whatever it is.

“We have to do a better job of finding the game early, making it easy and then not relying on double-digit comebacks because it’s taxing.”

On LeBron James’ performance against the Knicks:

“He’s been good, but tonight, I thought that was his best game for sure. I thought he was good all the way through tonight. I thought he got some downhill stuff. He used his size and knocked them around a little bit for some layups. I thought he obviously pushed the ball and got us organized. I thought he was a little quicker to make some decisions to shoot the 3-ball as well. And then, he obviously made those couple of big plays down the stretch.”

On how New York’s off-court opportunities can distract players after winning a championship:

“When you win a championship, especially in New York, you have all these different opportunities off the court that take place. You’re filming commercials, you’re having these different shows, you’re doing these different things. All these events are happening.

“You’ve got to try to narrow it back down and lock in on basketball because playing in New York, you can get a little bit taken away from the sport with all the activities that go along with being in New York City. But you have to now try to narrow it down back to basketball. Key in, lock in on basketball. Make it the main priority and build out from there.”

On why the Knicks deserved to celebrate their championship throughout the offseason:

“That’s normal. That’s a part of human nature, man. You win a championship for the New York Knicks. You kidding me? After 53 years, you gotta enjoy that. You will never be the first one to win it after 53 years ever again.

“So that energy, you have to capitalize on it. It’s just a matter of now being able to kind of channel that and now focus on basketball and lock in a little bit more.”

On whether the Knicks’ slow start is concerning:

“I’m not concerned. When you are the champions, man, every target is at your back. Every team’s gunning for you, so it’s tough to kind of get off to a great start the following year. I’m not concerned. I think it’s a matter of just kind of locking in and focusing a little bit more, and they’ll be okay.”

items.title: 76ers 98, Knicks 93: “Unfortunately it took us too long to show up tonight.”
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Last season, en route to a World Championship, the New York Knicks (2-4) took a pleasant detour in Las Vegas to collect the Emirates NBA Cup. The road to repeating the Cup win is rocky this season, with their Group B considered to be the toughest.

Tonight, they traveled to Pennsylvania to face the 76ers at the Xfinity Mobile Arena on a garish blue and gold cartoon court. This was their first Cup game of the season and the 482nd meeting between the two franchises. The Philadelphia 76ers (5-1) came in tied with Detroit for first place in the East. All night, the star-heavy squad showed the secret to their success so far this season—a stingy, sticky defense that limited New York to 32% perimeter shooting. Our heroes fell behind by double digits toward the end of the first quarter and stayed behind until the final two minutes of the game. Quoth Laurenpal, “Unfortunately it took us too long to show up tonight.” Despite a clutch bucket from Jalen Brunson (24 PTS, 8-22 FG) for the lead late in the fourth, Tyrese Maxey (27 PTS, 10-19 FG) and the Sixers were too strong to keep down. Your final: 98-93.

Through the first half of the first quarter, the home team had the edge, with Maxey, Joel Embiid (10 PTS, 7 RBS, 7 AST), LeBron James (20 PTS, 9 RBS, 8 AST), and VJ Edgecombe (13 PTS, 8 RBS) combining for 14 points. Across the floor, Karl-Anthony Towns (22 PTS, 12 RBS), OG Anunoby (9 PTS, 4-10 FG), Mikal Bridges (12 PTS, 3 STL, 5-8 FG), and Brunson had posted 11 for the visitors.

Part of the problem for our heroes was that Philly played an almost mistake-free opening frame, committing one foul and zero turnovers. And their defensive intensity—they’re top-five in the league—complicated every Knicks shot. When Tyler Kolek (2 PTS, 4 AST, 13 MIN) subbed in with about three minutes left, he was harassed into his first TO of the season. Further proof of that good D? The good guys shot just 27% in the first period.

On one sequence, Brunson dribbled against Maxey from 18 feet, left side, one-on-one. Maxey blocked him, but Cap retained the ball and swished a jumper on his second attempt. It was a rare instance of Maxey getting outplayed. He led all first-half scorers with 15 points. Brunson managed only seven points pre-intermission.

After a Philly timeout, Mike Brown sent in Landry Shamet (0 PTS, 0-3 FG, 16 MIN), Miles McBride (10 PTS, 4-8 FG, 24 MIN), and Andre Drummond (3 PTS, 6 RBS, 12 MIN). The guests missed five shots, during which time the hosts capitalized with interior scores. After surrendering eight unanswered points, the Knicks got relief when Josh Hart (7 PTS, 6 RBS, 31 MIN) delivered from deep. By the quarter break, the home team was up 29-21.

On to the second. Philly moved the ball well and was unafraid to drive the lane, as Maxey did with an emphatic throwdown. While Brunson rested—and Jose Alvarado sat out with a sprained ankle—Kolek continued to play. He gave up a second turnover. Cap checked back in around the seven-minute mark.

At the midway point, LeBron and Hart traded bombs from the perimeter. The differential reached 14 before the Knicks began to chisel it down.

McBride made some midrange shots from the elbow. It was nice to see a little more imagination in his usage, rather than just sticking him at the arc and waiting for a pass. He also grabbed a timely offensive board in the paint among Embiid and a couple of other big bodies.

Nevertheless, the Knicks couldn’t get a run going. A corner three by Bridges cut the gap to six, but Maxey chucked from deep for three of his own. In fitting fashion, Brunson couldn’t get open for a final shot, and the halftime buzzer buzzed without an attempt. Philly up, 53-44.

The Knicks had out-rebounded Philly (23-19) and shot slightly better from deep (32% to 29%), but Philly owned everything inside the arc. The Knicks took more than half their shots from deep and scored nothing on fast breaks, which is a tough way to keep pace while conceding so much inside. No Knick had reached double digits yet; KAT led the team with nine points.

Following intermission, Hart missed from deep, Bridges threw the ball to the front row, and Maxey scored five points. Philly went up by 14, matching its biggest advantage yet.

Finding the previous events intolerable, Brunson took the reins and commanded his squad on an 11-1 run. He scored seven straight during that burst, and Bridges redeemed his TO with a steal (ripping the ball out of Edgecombe’s mitts) and a longball. After that, Nurse needed a timeout for a breather and a regroup.

Whatever advice the coach imparted, it worked. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Anfernee Simons (21 PTS, 5-8 3PT, 31 MIN) hit triples, Philly tightened its defense, and LeBron attacked the cup. Soon enough, the Knicks trailed by ten again and gave us great concern about their ability to rally for a lead. After a Mike Brown timeout, two consecutive Shamet turnovers and another Simons jumper further pushed the score in the wrong direction. Too many one-and-dones were a problem. The Knicks wouldn’t quit and swung back, with McBride and Brunson reducing the hole to six, but a Simons bomb with five seconds to go closed the quarter at 77-68.

Jordan Clarkson, a sparkplug in Chicago, made his first appearance to start the final frame. Alongside him: Kolek, McBride, Anunoby, and Towns. They manufactured buckets, but surrendered them, too. Simons continued to rain buckets.

One of the surprising strengths of Clarkson’s game has been his offensive rebounding. When he flew through traffic to tip in a missed McBride three, it wasn’t quite a Game Four highlight, but it sliced the differential to three. That was the closest the team had been since midway through the first. But they taketh, they giveth. Embiid drilled a jumper at the other end, and with six-ish minutes left, Mike Brown needed a timeout.

Out of the timeout, Brown’s lineup was Brunson, Clarkson, Bridges, Hart, and Towns. The choice to go with Clarkson’s offense over Anunoby’s defense was a curious gamble. Both teams were careening up and down the court at top speed, even that geezer LeBron, and when KAT rifled a bomb, a mere two points separated the two teams.

In crunch time, Brunson had a look but bricked from deep. The ball came back to him, but LeBron worked him into a jam, with Jalen having to throw the ball off him out of bounds. After the inbound, Jalen had another chance—and connected from deep for their first lead since the opening minutes!

LeBron answered with a fadeaway at 1:10 to reclaim the lead. After Cap missed a floater, Edgecombe knocked down his first triple of the night. 94-90, 34 seconds remaining.

Cap got the ball again, iso-ing on Edgecombe, but slipped and turned his right ankle in a legitimately terrifying moment. Edgecombe was called for a ticky-tack foul (foot-to-foot contact). Brunson made one freebie. 94-91, 31 seconds. At the other end, Maxey hustled through traffic and missed on a contested layup, but ’Bron swept in for the putback. That put the score at 96-91 with 12 seconds on the clock. New York needed a miracle, but the gods were fresh out. Anunoby made a dunk, and Philly added two free throws. Ball game.

Back to work on Monday, at home against the Nets. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

items.title: Game Discussion Thread: Knicks at 76ers, October 30, 2026
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Sixers have gone 4-1 so far this season, and LeBron James has impressed in their locker room Bridge and Canasta games. Philly sits tied for first in the east behind Tyrese Maxey, with his 28 points per game, and Joel Embiid, who has stayed healthy for four of their five contests. Nick Nurse has his assortment of stars ranked top-five for defense. In late-breaking news, Jaylen Brown will miss the game due to left patellar tendiopathy, which my medical dictionary defines as “Fear of Knickerbocker.”

Tonight, they welcome the World Champion Knicks (2-3) in an Emirates Cup game. New York lost their opener to the Sixers, so let’s settle the score, eh? Game time is at 7 p.m. EST on Prime Video. This is your game thread. This is Liberty Ballers. Please don’t post large photos, GIFs, or links to illegal streams in the thread. Be excellent humans. And go Knicks!

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘He’s a great guy to play off’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Cup Basketball is back, and with that…

…so are your reigning Champs.

Here’s a bunch of quotes before today’s affair.

On Rick Brunson suggesting the Tyler Kolek-Jalen Brunson backcourt combination against Chicago:

“One of the things he suggested was throwing Kolek in the game with Jalen [Brunson].”

On Kolek’s performance in the Knicks’ comeback victory over the Bulls:

“Tyler had a big floor game for us.”

On Kolek’s role once Jose Alvarado return:

“Tyler is definitely going to keep playing while Jose is out. When he comes back, we’ll figure it out.”

On the need for avoiding the opening-night mistakes that doomed the Knicks:

“We just need to obviously not do what we did [the last time we played them].”

On avoiding turnovers and making smarter decisions as the Knicks’ backup point guard:

“Not trying to make the home run play. Just trying to get us in the offense, get the best shot for our team. It’s about being more mature in my game. Trying to take care of the ball, that’s what the team needs. When I go in there, I can’t be turning it over, I can’t be throwing it all over the floor. Got to get us in the offense, got to get us good shots.”

On playing alongside Jalen Brunson and benefiting from the defensive attention he attracts:

“We played together last season for stretches. He’s a great guy to play off. They’re going to double-team him, you get open shots.”

On the defensive challenges of playing in a two-point-guard lineup and staying ready for opportunities:

“Obviously it’s two smaller guards, so I have to compete harder on defense.

“You guys have seen [the double point guard]. It’s been successful in stretches, with Jose in the playoffs. With me a little bit in the NBA Cup. And then a couple games sprinkled in. But when coach is searching, trying to find something, everybody on the bench has to be ready for any situation.”

willingness to accept a discount:

“He will sign for less than his max contract. He’ll take a sizable discount. $70 plus million less, that’s something that he is not willing to do right now.”

items.title: Jalen Brunson named Athlete of the Year by the Philadelphia Sports Writers Association
items.author: Kento Kato
items.content:
2026 has been the year of Jalen Brunson. Shooting Stars champions, Conference Finals MVP, championship, Finals MVP, multiple ESPYs, and numerous media appearances, including Saturday Night Live and an upcoming appearance on his favorite show, Law and Order. But he’s not done yet. On Friday morning, Stefan Bondy of the New York Post reported that the point guard had been named the Professional Athlete of the Year by the Philadelphia Sports Writers Association. 

The press release released by the association, which consists of 17 members, highlights his incredible performance, ability to deliver in the clutch, and his leadership. 

“His skill, his leadership, and his connection to the Philadelphia basketball community all make him a deserving recipient of this honor. He plays his best when the stakes are the highest and has led his teams to championships at every level.” Mike Shute, president of the PSWA, said. “We are pleased to present him with this honor, as he joins a list of past winners such as Carl Lewis, Muhammad Ali, Wilt Chamberlain and Mike Schmidt.”

Brunson, who famously played at Villanova, will be honored at the 122nd Annual PSWA Awards Banquet next year on January 11th at the University of Pennsylvania. Funnily enough, the announcement also comes just hours before the Knicks take on the 76ers to kick off the 2026 NBA Cup.

items.title: NBA Cup Preview: Can the Knicks pass their first title defense?
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
Every time the Knicks take the floor in the 2026-27 season, they will do so as the hunted. They won just about every prize you could win last season, meaning they’ll never get a game without a bit of edge from an opponent.

Things won’t truly get real until the postseason for the real title defense, but the Knicks did hang a second banner to hang forever at the World’s Most Famous Arena.

That’s right. It’s time for the NBA Cup.

Last year, as an appetizer for June’s dramatics, the Knicks went 3-1 in group play, ultimately winning East Group C via head-to-head tiebreaker. They then took down the Raptors in Toronto, the Magic in Vegas, and came back from an 11-point third-quarter deficit to take home the NBA Cup after consecutive years of losing in the quarterfinals.

This year, they’ll face by far their hardest path to getting out of group play for the fourth consecutive year. Adam Silver has stacked the deck with a ridiculously competitive Group B that will be a war to get through. Even the wild card, which the Knicks have used to advance in the past, will be tough with likely few opportunities to run up the point differential.

Still, the Knicks are champs until they aren’t, even in a midseason tournament. Let’s meet the contenders:

Philadelphia 76ers (10/30, 7:30, Prime Video)

Tonight’s Cup opener in the City of Brotherly Love will be the Knicks’ second crack at the makeshift superteam that bested them on Opening Night in a back-and-forth affair.

The Sixers are one of those teams that I question how seriously they’re going to take the NBA Cup. Sure, there are some big measuring-stick games in this group, but with a lineup that they will be heavily load-managing throughout the season, one wonders if they’re going to take a condensed calendar that will require additional travel and even an extra game at the end of it. We saw how it burned out the Knicks last year.

To start the year, Philly is 4-1 with a very strange combination of a mediocre offense and… the best defense in basketball? What sense does that make? They’ve been healthy, only missing Joel Embiid and LeBron James for a single game on the dueling ends of a back-to-back. Despite playing Embiid for 39 minutes on Wednesday, he’s not on the injury report for Friday night.

While the Knicks might not care about the Cup anymore, it would behoove them to get revenge on Opening Night and not have to wait until February for another crack at these guys. We saw it with Detroit last year; the last thing we need is a year-long narrative of one team having our number.

Indiana Pacers (11/13, 7:00, Prime Video)

When the Knicks played the Pacers last season, it didn’t feel like the vibe of a rekindled rivalry between two teams that had played in consecutive postseasons. That was because Indiana was taking a voluntary gap year while Tyrese Haliburton rehabbed from an Achilles tear, managing injuries all season long and slipping to 19-63. Thankfully, it wasn’t rewarded in the lottery when they slipped to No. 5 and gave the pick to the Clippers.

That trade with the Clips did get them a certified big man that will swallow up boards in Ivica Zubac, someone who will be a tough cookie for Karl-Anthony Towns when these two teams finally face off in a heated atmosphere for the first time in almost two years.

The only problem? It doesn’t sound like Haliburton will be at the party.

He recently suffered a hamstring injury that will leave him out for at least two weeks. This game was just 16 days after that diagnosis, meaning the odds are slim that he’ll return based on what we know right now. That’ll diminish what we see, but we’re all aware of what Aaron Nesmith, Andrew Nembhard, and TJ McConnell can do for this team.

Indiana’s started the year off to an uneven 2-3 start, but Nembhard and Pascal Siakam are more than capable of shouldering the load in the coming weeks. I doubt they’ll be as special offensively as we’ve been accustomed to seeing without Haliburton, but they won’t be a pushover.

Going undefeated in this group will be hard, so this might be the Knicks’ best chance to pad their point differential. But to do that, the Knicks will need a full 48 minutes.

Cleveland Cavaliers (11/25, 7:30, MSG)

There are plenty of playoff rematches in this group. One of them is this Eastern Conference rematch the day before Thanksgiving at MSG, the site of the soul-crushing Game 1 comeback that killed the Cavs.

They’re off to an interesting 3-2 start, one that involves getting out to big leads every game, only to choke them immediately. They blew a 29-point lead to Philly, nearly blew a 20-point lead to Brooklyn, and had to rally late to beat Washington. The vibes are low there, if not just because nobody trusts Kenny Atkinson and James Harden has been abhorrent to start the year.

It’s hard to get a read on this game because the regular-season Knicks and the playoff Knicks are entirely different. It’s a team you expect to win, but we’re far enough out that we need to see what the situations look like.

Miami Heat (11/27, 7:00, Prime Video)

The Knicks’ 0-3 start got heavily publicized, but the Heat’s 0-4 start somehow made bigger waves after the massive offseason trade for Giannis Antetokounmpo.

The fit just looks clunky. He’s too similar to Bam Adebayo both offensively and defensively, which pushes Miami’s longest-tenured player to the periphery. That just can’t happen when your other scoring options are Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins. The defense will round into form (maybe?), but this is just a bleak offensive outlook.

That said, they could match up well against the Knicks, given their lack of size.

OG Anunoby and Towns are good, but they can’t play all game. Towns especially is extremely prone to getting in foul trouble, which is a disaster against Giannis. James Wiseman and/or Andre Drummond will be crucial to negating their paint advantage enough for the Knicks’ clear shooting advantage.

If this game is meaningful after good enough results in the first three games, it’s not a place I think the Knicks can get point differential out of. They’d need to just need a win. Beating Erik Spoelstra’s crew in Miami has always been hard for this crew.

PistonsRaptorsBucks

This could be a friskily fun group.

The Pistons are 4-1 with just that lone loss to the Knicks and feel like the favorite here. As we saw on Tuesday, things can get spooky outside of Cade Cunningham, and they’re without Jalen Duren for at least the first game, but Paul Reed has been more than capable in his absence.

The Raptors are also 4-1, but have a much bleaker outlook without Kawhi Leonard for the next few weeks. Their viability in this group will rely on Scottie Barnes’ offensive consistency. He’s gone from dropping 25 to dropping… zero at times. RJ Barrett and Immanuel Quickley look good!

Orlando is 1-3 with their lone win over the Knicks, but they’re going to be without Jalen Suggs and Paolo Banchero for the foreseeable future. This will likely not be their year after a trip to the semifinals last year.

The same can be said for the Bucks, who are just very underwhelming with Kyle Kuzma-led hoops. The Nets will put up a big fight with Julius Randle and Michael Porter Jr. capable of going off for 30 a night, but they’re not good enough defensively nor deep enough to have a real shot.

CelticsHawksBulls

The Celtics will be the definitive favorite to come out of the group, especially with Jayson Tatum looking like an early MVP candidate. Their three-point shooting is enough to carry them through a regular season, but can they figure out what’s up with Mitchell Robinson? He looks like a shell of himself.

Atlanta ran back most of the group that pushed the Knicks to six games last year, but added a bunch of defense in Lu Dort and Aaron Wiggins. They’re healthy, play with enough grit, and have the talent to sneak their way into the knockout round.

The Hornets are… better off without LaMelo? Despite injuries knocking out Kon Knueppel and Coby White, they’ve looked impressive to start the year under a new nucleus of Naz Reid and Brandon Miller. With Knueppel due back for the bulk of NBA Cup play, could their dynamic offense get them back in the saddle?

As we saw in a scare on Wednesday night, the Bulls have the ability to be frisky. Caleb Wilson has shown signs of brilliance, Norm Powell can score 35 on any given night, and they’ve gotten some damn good shot quality even if they aren’t always falling. They probably won’t do much, but in a four-game sample, anything is possible.

The Wizards have their Big 3 healthy: AJ Dybantsa, Trae Young, and Anthony Davis, but they haven’t played enough to tell if they’re a true threat. I lean no, as of now.

NuggetsRocketsMavericks

There are a lot of good teams in this group, but the Rockets look by far the best to start the year. If they stay healthy, they should have no problem. Dallas can steal some games with Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving, and the Nuggets have Nikola Jokic, but the outlook for the Suns and Jazz is bleaker. Utah’s injury bug is killing them, as Jaren Jackson Jr. will miss all of group play.

ThunderTimberwolvesPelicans

Are… are the Grizzlies the favorite? They’re 5-0 entering group play, while the two contenders in this group will be without key pieces. Anthony Edwards is likely done until the New Year, as is Cason Wallace and Jalen Williams for OKC. The Clippers and Pelicans are two of the worst teams in basketball, so the unlikely underdog in Memphis might actually do this.

SpursLakersWarriors

There’s a clear hierarchy here. The Spurs are the favorites; the Lakers are a Luka Doncic explosion away from winning this whole damn thing; the Blazers are extremely frisky and could make noise, and both the Warriors and Kings are dead in the water. O/U 100 FGA for Darius Acuff Jr. in group play.

Give me the Pistons to win the group and the Raptors to come in second, but miss the wild card.

The Knicks will not defend their cup title. There’s so much intensity with every game, not just in this group but league-wide, as the hunted. This feels like something that the regular-season merchants will succeed with, so congrats to the Cavs. This group will be cannibalized, so no wild card here

Boston is the easy pick to win the group, but I see the Hornets somehow finding a way to steal the wild card. They’ll win a game against the Bulls by 40 and pad the point differential with that offense, especially with Knueppel back.

The Rockets are a unit right now.

I don’t know what way this is going to go with how diminished OKC is. Screw it, lt’s go with the Grizzlies.

Spurs win the group, Blazers take the wild card via tiebreaker over the Lakers after a thrilling overtime win.

: In the East, the No. 1 seed Pistons grind down the plucky Hornets at home, while the Cavs stun the Celtics in Boston due to three-point variance. In the West, the top-seeded Rockets blow out the Blazers in Houston, while the Spurs host and beat the Thunder.

The Pistons and Cavs fight hard in a big playoff rematch, but it goes the same way with the Cavs going to the finals. Meanwhile, the Rockets take down the Spurs at home.

Finals: At Hinkle Fieldhouse, the Cavs will be able to operate with an essential home game. Unfortunately, as usual, the lights will be too bright. The Rockets win the 2026 NBA Cup, with Fred VanVleet scoring NBA Cup MVP.

items.title: Game Preview: Knicks at 76ers, October 30, 2026
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
Last weekend I went to a trading card show with my oldest son here in Germany. Lovely time, great fun. The old man got a nice Jordan, some Ewings and Shaqs, youngster found another Brunson for his collection. At one booth we were flipping through the dollar box as I noticed a rather ugly team logo on the vendor’s sweater. As he politely asked what we were looking for I told him about our love for the Knicks and then couldn’t help myself to make it clear we surely do not look for players of his unlikable squad.

The Philly fan laughed, I did too – just some ol’ good natured rubbing. As we discussed the early season I mentioned that he surely had an interesting year ahead of him. “We all know that it’s going to go south somehow”, he chuckled, referring to the bulky knees of his team’s center and other issues his franchise has grown accustomed to. Of course I knew what he was talking about; as you may remember, it was mostly the Knicks who tormented the little brothers from Philly in recent years. Yet I was still amazed at how defeated the nice man sounded regarding his team’s chances.

I’m sure you don’t have to look long before you find more obnoxious members of the Sixers fan species, especially after their surprisingly solid start to the season (4 wins, 1 loss). It also includes an opening night win against New York. Of course no Philly fan wants to hear about the asterik of getting the emotionally drained Knicks on Ring Night as a lot of people including their new star player made that game bigger than it actually was.

Knicks starting their NBA Cup defense in Philly

As fate would have it, the Sixers on Friday again have a chance to define themselves against a reigning champion, and again it will be your favorite basketball team. This time the Knicks start their title defense in the much-maligned NBA Cup, that test-tube baby of a basketball competition that clearly had its moments over the years yet feels extremely forced most of the time. No matter if you care about Adam Silver’s money grab or not the game against Philly will surely be an interesting one as it matches the Knicks against a potential playoff opponent and against one of their biggest rivals at the moment.

What we saw from the Sixers on Opening Night was a bit of a preview of their early season in general. They played some top-notch defense, helped by the switchability of a motivated LeBron James and the supposedly decent shape Joel Embiid has gotten himself in. Philadelphia has plenty of strong wings, and many of their guys thrive in the passing lanes. It gets them out on the break, as they have a top-5 pace in the NBA right now, and their assist-to-turnover ratio also sits right there with the best teams in the league.

Currently, that’s one of the only things they do well on offense, though. Exactly two players from their regular rotation shoot over 45 percent from the field right now; they get no offensive rebounds, and they do not shoot or hit a lot of threes. Even with all their scoring power, their half-court offense has mostly been driven by isolation. Every Philly star takes his turn, mostly with mixed results. Tyrese Maxey clearly has been the best of the brotherly bunch, scoring 28.4 points per game on 46.2 percent shooting.

76ers play strong defense yet run a clunky offense

The bad O and strong D have led to extreme ups and downs early for the newly assembled group, which partly was expected yet might also be a concern going forward. You sure wouldn’t feel that secure if your team got down by 29 against Cleveland in your home opener, then trail Detroit a few nights later by 21 in your only loss just to top it off by going into the 4th quarter down 13 against the Pacers sans Tyrese Haliburton and Ivica Zubac. Begrudgingly, we give them at least some credit for coming back.

Either way, the show must and will go on in Philadelphia. Only recently did we see LeBron complain about playing center and Joel Embiid about not playing at all – funny for one of the guys who basically invented the term load management. Jaylen Brown also made headlines talking about his relationship with Jayson Tatum, beef or no beef yet: “Maybe some lamb chops and gravy”. Uh, okay, we’ll chalk it up as just another instance of a guy trying to sound extremely smart and interesting yet doing the exact opposite.

For the Knicks it would definitely be smart to not get caught up in all that hoopla. Recently, they have found a much better rhythm on offense, and that will clearly be needed against the physical forces from Philly. Jose Alvarado might be coming back for this one; he is currently listed as a game-time decision. Limiting turnovers will be at a premium as New York does not want to run up and down with the 76ers, especially not on the road. When Nick Nurse tries to hide Embiid on Josh Hart, the Knicks have to punish it. Test the opponent’s communication on the backline with plenty of crisp backdoor cuts, ease the ball-handling pressure for Brunson, and hit your open shots. Sounds easy, I know. In the end, it’s only a game.

The vendor at the card show, and we definitely agreed on that. I’m not sure if he’s watching the battle this Friday; maybe he has another show to prepare for. One thing I know, though: I sure would love it if the Knicks gave him a reason to feel a little more defeated.

Who: New York Knicks (2-3) at Philadelphia 76ers (4-1)Date: Friday, October 30, 2026Place: Xfinity Mobile Arena, Philadelphia, PAFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

items.title: Knicks decline Pacôme Dadiet’s option
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
You’ll recognize the World Champion Pacôme Dadiet from his time spent cheering from the bench or dancing on a parade float. His babyface looks are unchanged since his NBA debut—much like his skills.

In a (not so) surprising move, the Knicks have declined to pick up the option for this important practice player. Scoopman Shams Charania reports that the Knicks “plan to decline Pacome Dadiet’s fourth-year option worth $5.37 million, sources tell ESPN.”

This money move will free up a little cap space for Leon Rose as he crunches contract numbers for Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart, and presumably Miles McBride and Tyler Kolek. The Frenchman will be an unrestricted free agent next summer.

Dadiet appeared in 18 games as a rookie, 29 as a sophomore, and for one minute of one game in the current campaign. He also played two seasons in the G League with the Westchester club. Late in his second season there, he delivered multiple 25–32-point games, including a 32-point outing with five boards, four dimes, two thefts, and a block.

Although he seemed to be improving in the minor leagues, he hasn’t shown it in his limited appearances at MSG. The best young NBA players demonstrate growth from year to year, with crisper floor movement, shot refinement, physical development, and increased BB IQ. Not so with Pac-Man. The barely 21-year-old will leave an important legacy in New York, however, even if this is indeed his final season with the club.

When selected with the 25th pick in the 2024 NBA Draft, Dadiet agreed to a four-year rookie-scale deal worth about $13.01 million rather than the more typical maximum scale amount near $13.9 million. First-round rookies can sign for as little as 80% or as much as 120% of the slotted amount. Dadiet took the minimum 80% for 2024-25, a first-year salary of roughly $1.81 million instead of around $2.71 million.

This created about $904,000 in extra flexibility under the 2024-25 second-apron hard cap. The Knicks also paid an $850,000 buyout to free him from his German club (Ratiopharm Ulm), but that overseas buyout did not count against the NBA salary cap.

Without that discount, the subsequent trade for Karl-Anthony Towns (which sent Julius Randle, Donte DiVincenzo, and other pieces to Minnesota, with Charlotte involved for salary matching) would have nudged New York over the second apron. The Towns acquisition as structured would have been impossible, at least in that form.

Later seasons of Dadiet’s deal moved closer to (or above) standard scale, but by originally “taking less,” he helped facilitate the acquisition of KAT, who helped deliver a championship to the city two years later.

The new season is still young—and so is he—but Dads already has a ring and some serious bragging rights. If the ride ends after this season, he’s got plenty to be proud of.

items.title: Praying for the healthy Knicks as we approach Día de Muertos
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
It’s not even Halloween, the NBA season is barely a week old, but the injury report already looks like something you’d expect to read in April.

Here in Mexico City, I can relate. You can feel in the air, both figuratively and literally. We’re just days — hours, if you push it — away from one of the biggest festivities in the country to take place this weekend. No need to explain what we celebrate, trying to bring back those who left us in the past to start just another chapter away from the land. If only for a little .

Meanwhile, in the NBA, it looks like stars are playing a very solid role in a performance mimicking this weekend’s celebrations. It’s not a few, but , who have already undergone surgery and be placed on the shelves for months on end, if not the whole year, outright.

Meanwhile, the New York Knicks are doing something that is starting to feel illegal, some sort of subterfuge competitive advantage in itself.

Being healthy. .

Now compare that with the rest of the league, where approximately 15 percent of players (s/o Keerthika!) were dealing with injuries or illnesses yesterday afternoon. Eleven former All-Stars were already expected to miss several weeks or longer just eight days into the season.

The NBA injury report is a hot

Obviously, the most concerning situation might be in Oklahoma City, where Jalen Williams underwent surgery to repair a fractured left fibula and reconstruct ankle ligaments following a fracture-dislocation and will only be by the team when the regular season . Gone for good, in other words. Descanse en paz, bendito. His teammate Cason Wallace also needs surgery after tearing the labrum in his left shoulder, and both will miss a hellaciously long time.

Minnesota’s Anthony Edwards underwent arthroscopic surgery on his right knee and could miss two months. Utah’s Jaren Jackson Jr. tore the MCL in his right knee and faces a six-to-eight-week absence. Indiana’s Tyrese Haliburton, already coming off a season lost to an Achilles injury, will miss at least two weeks with a hamstring strain. Orlando’s Paolo Banchero faces four to six weeks out with a high ankle sprain, while Toronto’s Kawhi Leonard is expected to miss multiple weeks because of swelling in his left knee. Elsewhere, Golden State is without Jimmy Butler III until potentially January or February, while Kristaps Porzingis remains away indefinitely with ongoing health concerns. Sacramento’s Ben Simmons and former Knickerbocker Ariel Hukporti suffered Achilles ruptures, and Washington’s Jamir Watkins is recovering from ACL surgery.

Hay más almas que cempasúchil en el sendero.

Somehow, the Knicks have avoided all of this

As Stefan Bondy of the New York Post noted, every member of the Knicks’ starting five reached the 65-game threshold in both 2024-25 and 2025-26. Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, and Karl-Anthony Towns have provided a level of continuity that most teams can only dream about.

Bridges hasn’t missed an NBA game in his career even though seemingly everybody wants him hitting the pine for a start, with his streak reaching 643 consecutive appearances on Wednesday. Towns and Anunoby, meanwhile, arrived in New York with considerable injury histories but have remained remarkably durable.

Per Bondy, the Knicks’ starting five led the NBA with 940 minutes together in 2024-25, finished second with 541 last season, and ranked first again through four games this year.

ESPN listed across on its injury report, with the San Antonio Spurs and the Memphis Grizzlies, , escaping .

Here’s the list.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Sugar’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
All of a sudden, the Knicks look scary.

Who would have thought after they won the championship four months ago lost three in a row!?

Here’s the latest as the guys rest up for their NBA Cup title-defending debut on Friday.

On why Mo Diawara and Pacome Dadiet haven’t played this season:

“It’s tough because going into the season early on, one of [the] things I wanted to experiment with is playing 10 or 10 ½ guys [as my rotation]. And Mo is in that mix. Mo and Pac. Give them different opportunities at different times. And we experimented with different stuff and our players not getting it done caused us to start off a little slow.

“So to get us on track, we’re going to hold the fort down with a veteran group of guys. Hopefully we get to the point sooner than later that I can start throwing those [young] guys out there.”

On continuing to experiment with the Knicks’ bench rotation:

“Our starting five is what it is. But everybody else after that, until we find something that’s working consistently, I’m going to try to give different guys opportunities.”

On Jalen Brunson overcoming his shooting struggles against Chicago:

“I wasn’t worried about that. He just seems like he always finds a way. And tonight we needed every single one of those. It definitely wasn’t a concern of mine.”

On the Knicks looking sluggish after arriving in Chicago at 2:30 a.m.:

“It was just a late game [Tuesday night]. I acknowledged that to our guys. It’s not an excuse. It’s the life of the NBA. So we have to find a way in situations like this, and our guys found a way. But you could tell we looked really, really sluggish.”

On Brunson’s determination, toughness and MVP-caliber ability:

“His will is unbelievable. His determination, man, it’s second to none. You look at this guy and he’s not 6-7, he’s not athletic, he’s not quick. I mean, you can go down the line in natural physical tools that a lot of guys have, but his determination, his spirit, his competitive spirit, his will, his toughness, especially his mental toughness, but his physical toughness, too, added with his skill set, it makes him an unbelievable basketball player. An MVP-caliber basketball player. I hope he gets recognition for that this year because his will is off the charts.”

On benching Mikal Bridges and using Tyler Kolek alongside Brunson on Wednesday:

“We just found a combination we went with. One of the things [assistant coach] Rick Brunson suggested was throwing Kolek in the game with Jalen. Just to give them a different look and get Jalen off the ball and put Tyler on the floor.

“Doing that, playing Jordan Clarkson extended minutes, Landry was playing well. Now there’s not much room. And the combination we had out there, we kept playing well. It was harder to go back to what we started with.”

On Karl-Anthony Towns continuing to shoot after injuring his left hand and wrist:

“He was still shooting that thang from 30 feet. So the wrist looked good to me.”

On whether the Knicks are generating good shots despite their early shooting struggles:

“The biggest thing is: are we getting good shots from the right people? Watching the film and watching the game, I think we are. We’ve had some pretty good looks from the right people at the right time that normally go in so I want them to keep shooting.”

On what Tyler Kolek needs to improve as the Knicks’ backup point guard:

“He’s gotta run the team. What I mean by that is, when you watch our games, when he goes on the floor, people get up into his chest when he’s trying to run our offense. He can’t get off the ball too early, if it’s just one guy. He’s gotta be able to go by that guy and get the guy off-balance and bring it back out and set our offense up and/or get by and make a play in the paint. He can’t let pressure bother him or disrupt our offense at all.

“And then defensively, he’s gotta be a pest. He’s gotta be nasty, not anything illegal or anything like that, just a guy that people wanna say ‘get off me, get off me,’ because he’s more than capable of doing that. He’s gotta play with some sort of force, particularly for his size.”

On the Knicks’ bench contributions in their comeback victory over Chicago:

“We got a lot of contributions from all across the board. I thought our bench was fantastic. Landry came off the bench and had 14 points, 4-for-7 from the three-point line was huge. Andre Drummond came off the bench and had 11 rebounds in 15 minutes. That was huge. Tyler hit three big threes, nine assists in 18 minutes. Zero turnovers; he’s just a ball mover. That was huge.

“And obviously our defensive player of the game, Jordan Clarkson. He was big for us. He had been on the shelf for a while. Not only was he big for us offensively, but he had two big steals for us during our run. Our bench was very good for us tonight.”

On overcoming his shooting slump and rediscovering his rhythm against the Bulls:

“I was happy to be able to kind of finally get over that hump. I feel like I was putting a lot of unnecessary commentary in my head. But seeing the ball go in the way it did, it put me out of my mental state and put me in a good flow state.”

On how he broke out of the slump:

“I switched a couple of things up.”

On his relationship with Derrick Rose and Rose’s son, P.J.:

“It’s crazy to see how old he is now. I’m thankful for the relationship I have with him and his family. I feel like the feeling is mutual. I’m happy to have (Derrick) as a mentor and someone I can talk to, and someone I look up to, as well.”

On his memories of growing up around Chicago basketball and attending Bulls games:

“So many memories. I remember the Eastern Conference finals with Derrick, when they lost to LeBron, and going to all of those games. I met Kobe here. I met countless players here. Just how loud the United Center was — it’s always going to be loud no matter the situation. So many memories. I remember exactly where I used to sit and everything. It was perfect.”

On remembering the late Stacey King and his support during Brunson’s high school years:

“I just want to say RIP to Stacey King, who we lost recently. He’s a person I knew when I was in high school out here. He supported our team a lot. His kids went to Stevenson.”

On the source of Josh Hart’s seemingly endless energy:

On the Knicks’ confidence in Jalen Brunson during clutch situations:

“We have a lot of confidence. What we’ve built as a team, Jalen (Brunson) at the end of games, knowing that he’s going to make shots. Then, everybody else doing the small things. We’re just competing to win.”

On Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns and OG Anunoby after facing the Knicks:

“Jalen Brunson cold. Then KAT is just––he’s huge, he’s huge, he just makes the right decision, can shoot, trail threes, just plays the basketball really well. Honestly, they’re just a good team. OG’s really good too, really physical, hard to go against, hard to score against, they just have a really well-rounded team.”

On Jordan Clarkson’s performance:

“Even Jordan Clarkson came the bench and finished it. He played really well.”

On facing the Knicks again in a few days:

“We get to play them again next week at their place. We’ll learn from this and hopefully we can go out there and get a win.”

On reports that James Dolan is unhappy with Knicks players over a potential White House visit:

“People have been a little bit stressed because the owner, James Dolan, has an attitude with players because they don’t want to go to the White House.”

On his opinion of Dolan and the reported disagreement:

“I don’t know whether this is true or not, but I’ll believe anything when it comes to James Dolan because he is a walking embodiment of petulance. This man is as petty as they come.”
